title: North America today
hookLine: Sikhs farm, drive, teach, heal and lead across Canada and the US

lines: A TRUCK AT A REST STOP.
MY DRIVER, MY TEACHER, MY NURSE.
cards: Five in the morning on an interstate. A long-haul truck pulls into a rest stop, and the driver, in a neat turban, stretches and heads for coffee.
A few hours later, in a valley full of orchards, a farmer checks the peach trees. In a classroom, a teacher writes the day's date on the board. In a hospital, a nurse takes a pulse.

In a city council chamber, a member stands to speak. Each of them is a Sikh, and the people they pass may not think about that at all. They just think: that's my driver, my farmer, my kid's teacher, my nurse.

teach.b: First, the work. Across Canada and the United States, Sikhs farm, drive trucks and taxis, run shops, teach, heal and serve in public office. Some families have been here for generations; some arrived last year.
Second, the teaching under the work. The Sikh way calls this kirat karni, earning by honest work.

teach.h: ANG 1376: HANDS AT WORK, MIND WITH GOD.
teach.b: Among the saloks at Ang 1376 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Namdev, a calico printer by trade, tells his friend Trilochan: with your hands and feet, do all your work, and keep your mind with the Pure One.
A paycheck isn't separate from the spiritual life; it's one of its places. Third, the open door. Beside honest work, the Sikh way asks for vand chakna, sharing what you earn.
Gurdwaras across the continent serve langar to anyone who walks in.
Sikh volunteers have cooked for neighbors after storms and fires, and handed out meals in parking lots and stadiums. Nobody is asked what they believe before they eat. Fourth, the word.

Nobody is handed the title neighbor. It grows slowly, from showing up: the driver who waves at the same diner every week, the farmer who lends a ladder over the fence, the nurse who remembers your mother's name.
Sikhs in North America live it in ordinary ways, at the next desk, the next farm, the next house.

how: Sikhs in Canada and the US practice kirat karni, honest work, alongside vand chakna, sharing, and gurdwaras serve langar to anyone who comes in.

o: honest work, earning a living by fair means
sharing what you earn with those in need
a trade passed down from parent to child

games.q: work and neighbors — tap the pairs.
p: Namdev: hands at work, mind with God

s: in the Ang 1376 salok, work and remembering God are kept apart
Namdev keeps both: hands and feet at work, the mind with the Pure One.
gurdwaras ask what you believe before you eat
langar is served to anyone who walks in.
vand chakna means sharing what you earn
beside kirat karni, honest work, the Sikh way asks for sharing.

games.q: a storm has knocked out power across your town, and your gurdwara still has a working kitchen. what do you do?
o: keep it for the sangat only.
cook for whoever needs a meal.
close until the power is back.
games.why: Sikh volunteers have cooked for neighbors after storms and fires; langar doesn't check who you are.

practice: Picture the people around where you live or work: the one next door, the one across the hall, the driver, the cashier, the person who fixes things.
Choose one, by name or just by face, and on each breath out thank them silently for one thing that makes your days easier. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you do.

wordCard.voice: Kirat. Honest work, lived out by Sikhs who farm, drive, teach, heal and lead across Canada and the US today. Today's word.

orig.note: kirat, honest work; kirat karni is earning a living honestly.

carryVoice: Your line: neighbors. Honest work, and a meal shared with whoever lives next door. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 1376 (Salok Kabir 213: Namdev to Trilochan, do all your work with hands and feet, keep the mind with the Pure One)
